extracted.intended_audience: readers/scholars of Jefferson's correspondence and early U.S. constitutional politics
extracted.subtask_description: Extract Jefferson's substantive recommendations and evaluative principles about constitutional design, governance, and related diplomatic/trade negotiation practice as expressed in his 1787–1788 letters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government organized into legislative, judiciary, and executive
rubrics_metrics.description: "I like the organization of the government into legislative, judiciary, and executive.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jefferson states approval of separation of powers as a core principle for framing a government that will operate peaceably without continual recurrence to State legislatures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislature's power to levy taxes and direct election of the greater House
rubrics_metrics.description: "I like the power given the legislature to levy taxes, and for that reason solely, I approve of the greater House being chosen by the people directly.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He accepts direct election of the larger legislative chamber to preserve the fundamental principle that the people are not to be taxed but by representatives chosen immediately by themselves; he concedes that such a house "will be very far inferior to the present Congress" in capacity but values the principle of direct representation for taxation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve principle that people are taxed only by their immediate representatives
rubrics_metrics.description: "the fundamental principle, that the people are not to be taxed but by representitives chosen immediately by themselves.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jefferson treats this as a paramount constitutional safeguard that justifies structural choices even at the cost of legislative effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compromise between great and little States (equal vs proportional influence)
rubrics_metrics.description: "I am captivated by the compromise of the opposite claims of the great and little States, of the latter to equal, and the former to proportional influence.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He endorses the Connecticut-style compromise as a valuable balance reconciling competing state-size interests in a federal constitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voting by persons instead of by States
rubrics_metrics.description: "I am much pleased, too, with the substitution of the method of voting by persons, instead of that of voting by States:",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jefferson favors person-based voting over state-based voting as part of the new constitution's improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive negative (veto) together with a third of either House
rubrics_metrics.description: "I like the negative given to the Executive, conjointly with a third of either House; though I should have liked it better, had the judiciary been associated for that purpose, or invested separately with a similar power.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He supports an executive veto coupled with a legislative minority check, but recommends judicial participation or a separate similar power for the judiciary as an improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of an explicit bill of rights
rubrics_metrics.description: "First, the omission of a bill of rights... I consider all the ill as established, which maybe established. I have a right to nothing, which another has a right to take away; and Congress will have a right to take away trials by jury in all civil cases... Let me add, that a bill of rights is what the people are entitled to against every government on earth, general or particular; and what no just government should refuse, or rest on inference.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jefferson critiques omission of an explicit declaration of rights and lists concrete protections that should be provided rather than left to inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific rights to be secured in a bill of rights
rubrics_metrics.description: He enumerates specific protections: "freedom of religion, freedom of the press, protection against standing armies, restriction of monopolies, the eternal and unremitting force of the habeas corpus laws, and trials by jury in all matters of fact triable by the laws of the land, and not by the laws of nations.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are given as the minimum substantive components Jefferson believes a bill of rights should clearly and unambiguously guarantee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve trials by jury in civil matters of fact
rubrics_metrics.description: "trials by jury in all matters of fact triable by the laws of the land, and not by the laws of nations.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jefferson warns against reducing States that have preserved jury trial to the lower standard of those that have dispensed with it; he treats jury trial in factual matters as a "sacred palladium of liberty."

rubrics_metrics.name: Support principle of rotation in office, especially for President
rubrics_metrics.description: "The second feature I dislike, and strongly dislike, is the abandonment, in every instance, of the principle of rotation in office, and most particularly in the case of the President.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jefferson argues that permitting indefinite re-election makes the first magistrate effectively an officer for life, inviting foreign and domestic interference and factionalism; he favors frequent change to reduce the stakes of elections and prevent entrenchment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fear that infrequent elections increase risk of lifelong incumbency
rubrics_metrics.description: "It may be said, that if elections are to be attended with these disorders, the less frequently they are repeated the better. But experience says, that to free them from disorder, they must be rendered less interesting by a necessity of change.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He reasons that shorter terms and rotation reduce incentives for foreign powers and factions to invest resources in securing a particular leader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow appeals on matters of fact as well as law (concern over omissions)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Smaller objections are, the appeals on matters of fact as well as law; and the binding all persons, legislative, executive, and judiciary, by oath, to maintain that constitution.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jefferson lists appeals on matters of fact (not just law) and mandatory oaths to uphold the constitution as points of concern—implying careful consideration of appellate scope and compulsion by oath.

rubrics_metrics.name: Educate and inform the people as the best engine to preserve liberty and order
rubrics_metrics.description: "Educate and inform the whole mass of the people. Enable them to see that it is their interest to preserve peace and order, and they will preserve them.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jefferson argues that information and education of the populace are superior to increasing governmental energy for preventing insurrections and preserving liberty; he views a virtuous, informed majority as the surest reliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Will of the majority should prevail, with expectation of amendment if needed
rubrics_metrics.description: "After all, it is my principle that the will of the majority should prevail. If they approve the proposed constitution in all its parts, I shall concur in it cheerfully, in hopes they will amend it, whenever they shall find it works wrong.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He endorses majority rule tempered by the prospect of future amendment as the mechanism for correcting defects; this reliance assumes a virtuous citizenry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard against instability of laws—require a waiting period before passage
rubrics_metrics.description: "I think it would be well to provide in our constitutions, that there shall always be a twelvemonth between the engrossing a bill and passing it: that it should then be offered to its passage without changing a word: and that if circumstances should be thought to require a speedier passage, it should take two thirds of both Houses, instead of a bare majority.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jefferson prescribes a constitutional procedural safeguard to reduce legislative instability: a one-year waiting/review period unless a two-thirds supermajority votes to accelerate passage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal taxation structure suggestion: imposts to Congress, direct taxation to States
rubrics_metrics.description: "Would it not have been better to assign to Congress exclusively, the article of imposts for federal purposes, and to have left direct taxation exclusively to the States? I should suppose the former fund sufficient for all probable events, aided by the land office.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a principle of fiscal federalism, Jefferson suggests concentrating customs/imposts at the federal level while leaving direct internal taxation to states, believing customs revenue plus land sales would suffice for federal needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diplomatic discretion: avoid interceding where it would require repealing foreign law
rubrics_metrics.description: In discussing Captain Thomas: "For me to ask that this vessel shall be received, would be to ask a repeal of the law... It would not be right for me to strengthen that jealousy.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jefferson advises diplomatic restraint—do not press a foreign minister to suspend or repeal a foreign country's law on behalf of a private citizen when such a request would be inappropriate or counterproductive to broader relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade-negotiation principle: avoid duties that destroy domestic industry viability
rubrics_metrics.description: In arguing about whale-oil duties Jefferson wrote that a duty would "oblige the masters of vessels to enter their cargoes, for the information of government" and that he urged suppression of duties on whale-oil because "if the duty fell on the consumer, he would choose to buy vegetable oils; if on the fisherman, he could no longer live by his calling... and thus those fishermen would be shifted out of a scale friendly to France, into one always hostile.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When negotiating trade terms, avoid imposing duties that make domestic producers uncompetitive and thereby push production and allegiance toward rival markets; consider economic incentives and labor mobility in setting tariffs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of entrepôt rights to create near-free trade advantages
rubrics_metrics.description: "Article 10. The right of entrepôt... is almost the same thing, as the making all their ports, free ports for us... The communication between the entrepôt and the country is not interrupted by continual search... which has proved so troublesome to the inhabitants of our free ports...",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jefferson values entrepôt status (free-port-like privileges with less interference) to ease trade and reduce burdensome searches that harm commerce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suppress monopolies detrimental to trade (example: spermaceti candle monopoly)
rubrics_metrics.description: "A company had silently, and by unfair means, obtained a monopoly for the making and selling spermaceti candles: as soon as we discovered it, we solicited its suppression, which is effected by this clause.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In commercial negotiation and policy, identify and suppress monopolies obtained by unfair means to restore competitive access for foreign or domestic merchants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naturalization of American ships and citizens in host markets as gradual policy objective
rubrics_metrics.description: "the idea... of naturalizing American bottoms, and American citizens in France and in its foreign possessions... Once established here, and in their eastern settlements, they may revolt less at the proposition to extend it to those westward. They are not yet, however, at that point; we must be contented to go towards it a step at a time, and trust to future events for hastening our progress.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jefferson recommends pursuing gradual steps toward reciprocal naturalization and commercial privileges to embed U.S. maritime interests and advance trading rights incrementally rather than all at once.
